Orwell was an interesting experience, with a lot of potential and promise. I will say that I did enjoy the game for the most part, however, there are some glaring details which ruined it for me. 

The game relies on you (the investigator) uploading particular parsed sections of text to the server (Orwell), which means that whenever you come across a piece of information which is a "trigger" for want of a better term, it is highlighted - regardless of its relivence (and some information is totally surplus to requirement, a lot in one case). This means that most of the information which you read through, including important plot points, or interesting backstory, is largely irrelivent and the player (or at least I did) found myself just slowly scrolling to the bottom of every document to highlight all the options before I read anything at all. This is especially clear when investigating information which contradicts other information which has not been disclosed yet (marked by yellow highlighting instead of blue), as it will always be yellow, even if you have access to but haven't discovered the other piece of information yet - which unless the investigator is psychic, makes zero sense. A shame, since this dulls enthusiasm for what could otherwise be an engaging plot.

While processing this information you are presented with multiple occasions where information would be important to the case, but you cannot add it to your current file or create a new file because the game is not ready for you to do so. You will then later come back to re-read and submit this data after the game tells you the information you already noticed is important. This is irritating and makes the player feel like mommy is holding their hand through the entire experience, rather than allowing them to work on their own initiative. Although on reflection, this is most likely because the order in which the data is presented to you is not well organised from a storytelling perspective.

Attention to detail is somewhat lacking for a detective game also, as on multiple occasions you are directed to a forum which is occasionally updated with new articles to peruse. Unfortunately, when these articles are "published" the game does not update the "last logged in" sections of the user's profiles, which creates confusion over the timeline [spoiler]especially since this becomes important later in the story[/spoiler].

However, the largest problem is that there are several key events which the game does not provide you enough information to correctly answer (and there is a correct answer), which leads to the player essentially taking a wild guess as to which of the options is the correct one. If you are fortunate, you will get the result which you were looking for - if not... well you'll have to go through the entire game again from the beginning, as the game auto-saves after every piece of information you upload.

Overall, Orwell is a thought-provoking and mostly enjoyable game, but it does have it's flaws. If you can overlook them however, you will appreciate the intention of the developer. At this point I have to decide if I recommend Orwell or not, and it is difficult...

I'm divided about Orwell. 

It's original. It's fascinating. It's deep and intellectually engaging. 

It's also a point and click game, which is my least favourite genre. Orwell requires the player to read lots of information and click everything, often randomly, to discover the facts and evidence to allow events to proceed. What that translates to in real terms is long stretches of tedious, patience-testing reading and clicking. Not really my thing. 

For those reasons, I was very tempted to quit early in the game; however, as time went on I found the experience more and more engaging. I found plenty to enjoy and applaud and played it through to the end (admittedly, through gritted teeth at times). The ambition, the storyline, the interesting mechanics, the excellent cast and the consequential nature of the choices to be made are all worthy of note, and any game that tries to do something new and interesting should be applauded.

[h1][url=store.steampowered.com/app/491950/Orwell_Keeping_an_Eye_On_You/]Orwell[/url] presents a decent diminutive mystery with pertinent social commentary through a very unique, novel yet straightforward approach to interactive storytelling.[/h1]

The game first asks you to create an investigator profile through its polished interface, effectively recruiting you in the ranks of Orwell, followed by a stylish low-poly security footage opening that sets the stage for the ongoing investigation. Your role is essentially to play the human element in what would otherwise be an extremely complex data mining algorithm in a surveillance system.

Gameplay in many ways feels like browsing through restrained web pages obtained through a very limited portion of the internet. You select which datachunks to upload to Orwell's server, which in turn unlock more related headlines, websites, restricted documents, private emails, bank accounts, and eventually tap into phone and text conversations between suspects.

New bookmarks just appear by themselves as revealed by your adviser. You don't have any actual research to do, all important clues are automatically highlighted, and as such the game first appears to be completely linear and rather easy. There is initially no clear reason not to upload data other than rare instances with conflictual information, where only one of two bits can be sent.

Then it gets a bit more complex and the story evolves into a satisfyingly more sophisticated mystery with multiple threads to investigate. You can decide to withhold information that you judge inadequate or untrue, and your choices can have pretty severe consequences in some cases. While there are few or no time sensitive actions, tension builds up a lot in the final chapter where you have a limited number of uploads available before a major event triggers.

There is no undo and your decisions clearly define paths that lead to multiple endings. One-way conversations with your adviser also create a pretty unique relationship.

Be prepared for lots and lots of reading. The game features sparse audio and pleasant low-poly aesthetics, but too few rendered footage and no voice overs.

The game's world also feels relatively small scale with only about a dozen significant characters in the story, despite a background of terrorism and international tension. Another odd thing is when you gain access to a suspect's PC or smartphone, only a handful of files are shown. This limited scope nevertheless keeps things manageable.

The mechanics are buggy. There are several instances where if you fail to make a specific decision or if you do so in an unintended order, the game will not let you go any further and you get no clues that there's a bug until you realized that you've exhausted all possible resources and see that the game just won't move forward.

Orwell has definitely made it onto my list of indie favorites. One of the most interesting and engaging games I've played in a long time.

[b]Story[/b]
The story and characters are well written, realistic, and relatable. The pacing is perfect and each chapter will leave you anxious to get into the next one. The world has depth and lives and breathes. Your actions feel as though they carry real weight with consequences that follow you. This is the sort of story that you'll think about and speculate about even when you're not playing. It's obvious a lot of thought was put into Orwell.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
I think it's fair to say Orwell is more of an interactive novel than a game. But that by no means is a mark against it.

Gameplay is simple but effective. You play as an investigator trying to solve a recent bombing using whatever online information, public or private, is made available to you. When you come across information that your system (named Orwell) recognizes as relevant to one of your target persons, it becomes highlighted and you can choose to upload it to Orwell's database where your superiors can then see it and act on it.

But this surveillance system isn't perfect. Sometimes conflicting or irrelevant information will be highlighted and you'll have to use your best judgement when choosing what to upload. I won't explain more in depth than that - I think the rest of the gameplay is best experienced when you discover it yourself. But I promise the gameplay isn't the mindless drag and drop that it might seem.

And what I thought was neat is that while some aspects of the gameplay might seem arbitrary or slightly confusing at first, these mechanics have a real canon, in-world explanation that is revealed as you progress. The gameplay really feels like part of the story here.

[b]Performance[/b]
It'll probably run on just about anything.

[b]Length[/b]
There are five chapters, each of which took me 45-60 minutes or so. Some people might complete it faster since I'm the methodical, read-everything-before-moving-on sort (which is rewarding with Orwell). Very little (if any) replay value though. Some people might recommend playing it all in one sitting, but I would say taking day or two long breaks like I did is the way to go.

[b]Price[/b]
Full price at the time of this review is $10. I was able to grab Orwell while it was temporarily free. $10 seems a little bit steep at first, but considering the ~5 hours I got out of it and the impression it left on me, I would say Orwell is easily worth that much. You can probably also count on Orwell going on sale or getting it cheap in a bundle if you're still on the fence.

[b]Conclusion[/b]
Get it. If you enjoy indie games, get it. If you like a good detective story, get it. If surveillance or digital privacy even remotely interest you (which they should), get it.

Orwell puts you in the shoes of an investigator using a new surveillance system called Orwell that allows him to spy into the lifes of citizens in order to investigate recent terrorists bombings.
 
My review :
Graphics : 1 point. The game is visually pleasant, but the art style was a bit off to me at some point. It was ahrd to tell if some character portraits were actually really for this character. 
Gameplay : 2 points. A very easy game to play, consist of clicking and drag and drop... but be careful what you put into the system or you might easily do something you will regret. 
Sound : 1 point. The music was pleasant, The main theme got stuck in my head for quite some time. I would have liked the game to feature voice acting. It would have been better for the immersion and give more weight to the characters.
Replay value : 2 points. Once finished i wanted to go back to take a different approach to some situation. After rereading elements i saw how i could took a different path and maybe put myself at ease with some choices i regretted. Took me about 4 hours to complete on a first run, but im sure i will have to spend another 4 to get achievements and see the different endings.
Entertainment value : 2 points.  Its a game well designed, working flawlessly. A scenario with a lot of twists. The game give you a lot to think about, especially if you are interested in political topics like security and mass surveillance.

so far so good

The Gameplay:
The style of gameplay is certainly unorthodox from your standard games, but it is easy to understand and even empowering. You essentially link relevant information regarding a person or event and depending on how you do that, certain events will play out.

The Story:
You operate a special hacking suite provided by the government to pry into someone's life and essentially build a report about the person and their activities. There is person receiving your report and they act on what you provide. It was interesting to follow and felt real enough to hit home a lot of times. 

The Visuals:
The art choice was interesting for the characters giving them a somewhat pixelated look. The actual HUD was very nice to look at and easy to use. 

The Sound:
The soundtrack was distinct and set a nice atmosphere for the work you are about to do. Nothing else really stood out save for some of the menu noises which were neat. 


The Experience:
When getting this game, I thought I would find it mildly entertaining. I was not prepared for how into the game I would end up getting. I was so enthralled with the way the investigation pans out that I got a notepad and started jotting down relevant info and dates to make sure I could solve the case. 

It has a decent amount of replayability since you can choose different options which very satisfyingly changes the context of the rest of the story. The game hit that sweet spot of not being too short nor being too long. Overall I feel Orwell did a good job of putting you in the seat of the Investigator and keeping the game and story fresh.

This game sure stays true to it's name.

In short: Orwell is a Thought (heh) provoking experience that you need to play if you love a good story.
It starts off intruiging and quickly ramps up more and more, leaving you at the edge of your seat.

Overall I'd give this game a solid 1884/10.

I got this for free like a lot of other people, and I was immediately enticed by the concept - George Orwell's books such as 1984 which involve "Big Brother" themes are great and it was neat to see this translated into a video game. The game is a pretty linear game in which you gather information on suspects and try to connect the dots. Towards the end of the game you are given less direction and you must figure out things a bit more independently - for example, there is an important part of the game where you are only allowed to save a few pieces of information which could make or break the police's investigations. It's a well executed game with some great plot twists and my only wish is that it could have had more content. This is answered in part by "Ignorance is Strength" (essentially a standalone sequel) but it does leave the question of, say, custom levels open because there is massive potential for some thrilling fan-made episodes.

TL:DR - Linear investigation game with short but sweet rollercoaster plot tackling the issue of privacy and surveillance. Recommended at any price - not just free or on sale.
